prompt: How are alkyllithium reagents, RLi, prepared?

choices.text: By reaction of an alkyl halide with lithium metal
By reaction of an alkyl halide with lithium iodide
choices.why: Lithium metal is needed. LiI is a by-product when alkyllithiums react with CuI.

choices.text: By reaction of an alkane with lithium metal
choices.why: Like Grignard reagents, alkyllithiums are made from alkyl halides; an alkane has no halogen.

choices.text: By reaction of a Grignard reagent with copper(I) iodide
choices.why: It is alkyllithiums that react with CuI, and that reaction makes Gilman reagents, not RLi.

explanation: Alkyllithium reagents are prepared much like Grignard reagents, by reaction of an alkyl halide with lithium metal: 1-bromobutane and 2 equivalents of lithium in pentane give butyllithium and LiBr. Alkyllithiums are both nucleophiles and strong bases.

prompt: How are lithium diorganocopper (Gilman) reagents, R2CuLi, made?

choices.text: From an alkyllithium and copper(I) iodide in diethyl ether
From an alkyl halide and copper metal in water
choices.why: Gilman reagents are made from alkyllithiums and CuI in ether.

choices.text: From a Grignard reagent and lithium iodide in ether
choices.why: The starting materials are an alkyllithium and copper(I) iodide.

choices.text: From a boronic acid and a palladium catalyst with base
choices.why: Boronic acids and palladium are used in the Suzuki–Miyaura reaction, not to make R2CuLi.

explanation: Alkyllithiums react with copper(I) iodide in diethyl ether to give lithium diorganocopper compounds, R2CuLi, often called Gilman reagents. For example, 2 CH3Li + CuI → (CH3)2CuLi + LiI.

prompt: How many equivalents of methyllithium react with one equivalent of copper(I) iodide to make lithium dimethylcopper, (CH3)2CuLi?
explanation: The Gilman reagent carries two methyl groups on copper, so 2 equivalents of CH3Li are used: 2 CH3Li + CuI → (CH3)2CuLi + LiI.

prompt: Gilman reagents undergo coupling with which organohalides?

choices.text: Chlorides, bromides and iodides, but not fluorides
Fluorides only
choices.why: Fluorides are the one class that doesn't couple.

choices.text: Iodides only
choices.why: Chlorides and bromides couple too; only fluorides don't.

choices.text: Fluorides, chlorides, bromides and iodides alike
choices.why: Fluorides don't undergo the coupling reaction.

explanation: Lithium diorganocopper compounds undergo a coupling reaction with organochlorides, bromides and iodides, but not fluorides. One alkyl group from the reagent replaces the halogen, forming a new carbon–carbon bond.

prompt: Lithium dimethylcopper, (CH3)2CuLi, reacts with 1-iododecane. What hydrocarbon forms?

choices.text: Undecane
Decane
choices.why: A methyl group, not a hydrogen, replaces the iodine, so the chain grows by one carbon to 11.

choices.text: Dodecane
choices.why: Only one of the two methyl groups is transferred; the other leaves as CH3Cu.

choices.text: Icosane, from two decyl groups joining
choices.why: The new C–C bond joins a methyl group from the Gilman reagent to the decyl group.

explanation: One alkyl group from the Gilman reagent replaces the halogen of the organohalide, forming a new C–C bond. A methyl group replaces the iodine of 1-iododecane (10 carbons), giving undecane (11 carbons) in 90% yield, along with LiI and CH3Cu.

prompt: What forms when iodobenzene reacts with lithium dimethylcopper?

choices.text: Toluene (methylbenzene)
Benzene
choices.why: A methyl group, not a hydrogen, replaces the iodine.

choices.text: No product, because aryl halides don't couple
choices.why: The coupling works with aryl and vinylic halides as well as alkyl halides; iodobenzene gives toluene in 91% yield.

choices.text: Iodotoluene, with the methyl added next to the iodine
choices.why: The methyl group replaces the iodine rather than a ring hydrogen.

explanation: The coupling reaction can be carried out on aryl and vinylic halides as well as on alkyl halides. A methyl group from lithium dimethylcopper replaces the iodine of iodobenzene, giving toluene (91%).

prompt: trans-1-Iodo-1-nonene reacts with lithium dibutylcopper. How many carbon atoms does the coupling product have?
explanation: A butyl group (4 carbons) replaces the iodine on the 9-carbon chain, giving a 13-carbon product: trans-5-tridecene (71%). The coupling works on vinylic halides as well as alkyl halides.

prompt: Muscalure, the sex attractant of the common housefly, is made commercially by coupling cis-1-bromo-9-octadecene with lithium dipentylcopper. How many carbon atoms does muscalure have?
explanation: A pentyl group (5 carbons) replaces the bromine on the 18-carbon chain: 18 + 5 = 23 carbons. Muscalure is (9Z)-tricosene.

prompt: How does the coupling of a Gilman reagent with an organohalide take place?

choices.text: A triorganocopper intermediate forms, then couples and loses RCu
By a typical polar nucleophilic substitution
choices.why: The section states that the coupling is not a typical polar nucleophilic substitution reaction.

choices.text: By a radical chain reaction like NBS bromination
choices.why: No radical chain is involved; the mechanism goes through a triorganocopper intermediate.

choices.text: Through an organopalladium intermediate and a boronic acid
choices.why: That describes the Suzuki–Miyaura reaction.

explanation: The mechanism of the coupling reaction involves initial formation of a triorganocopper intermediate, followed by coupling and loss of a mono-organocopper, RCu. It is not a typical polar nucleophilic substitution reaction.

prompt: What does the Suzuki–Miyaura reaction couple?

choices.text: An aromatic or vinyl boronic acid with an aromatic or vinyl organohalide
An alkyl boronic acid with an alkyl halide, using a palladium catalyst
choices.why: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction doesn't work with alkyl substrates.

choices.text: A lithium diorganocopper reagent with an aromatic organohalide
choices.why: That is diorganocopper coupling. The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction uses a boronic acid, R–B(OH)2.

choices.text: Two aromatic organohalides, joined with the help of magnesium metal
choices.why: One partner is a boronic acid, and the reaction uses a palladium catalyst and a base.

explanation: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction couples an aromatic or vinyl substituted boronic acid, R–B(OH)2, with an aromatic or vinyl substituted organohalide in the presence of a base and a palladium catalyst.

prompt: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction is less general than diorganocopper coupling. Why is it preferred when possible?

choices.text: It uses catalytic metal, and palladium is less toxic than copper
It works with alkyl halides as well as aryl and vinyl halides
choices.why: It doesn't work with alkyl substrates; that is what makes it less general.

choices.text: It needs no base or other additive, unlike diorganocopper coupling
choices.why: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction is run in the presence of a base.

choices.text: It uses a full equivalent of palladium, so it goes to completion
choices.why: It uses only a catalytic amount of palladium. Diorganocopper coupling is the one that uses a full equivalent of metal.

explanation: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction doesn't work with alkyl substrates, but it is preferred when possible because it uses only a catalytic amount of metal rather than a full equivalent and because palladium compounds are less toxic than copper compounds.

prompt: What is the first step in the mechanism of the Suzuki–Miyaura reaction?

choices.text: The aromatic halide reacts with the palladium catalyst to form an organopalladium intermediate
The boronic acid reacts directly with the aromatic halide to form the biaryl
choices.why: The halide first reacts with the catalyst. The boronic acid reacts with that organopalladium intermediate in the second step.

choices.text: A diarylpalladium intermediate decomposes to the biaryl and regenerates the catalyst
choices.why: That is the last step of the cycle, not the first.

choices.text: The aromatic halide reacts with copper(I) iodide to form a triorganocopper intermediate
choices.why: Triorganocopper intermediates belong to diorganocopper coupling, not the palladium-catalyzed reaction.

explanation: Figure 10.7.1: (1) the aromatic halide, ArX, reacts with the catalyst to form an organopalladium intermediate; (2) that intermediate reacts with the aromatic boronic acid; (3) the diarylpalladium intermediate decomposes to the biaryl product plus regenerated catalyst.

prompt: What kind of compound is the Suzuki–Miyaura reaction particularly useful for preparing?

choices.text: Biaryls, which have two linked aromatic rings
Alkanes made by joining two alkyl groups
choices.why: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction doesn't work with alkyl substrates.

choices.text: Alkyl halides made from alcohols
choices.why: The reaction forms C–C bonds. Alkyl halides come from alcohols with HX, SOCl2 or PBr3 (Section 10.5).

choices.text: Grignard reagents made from aryl halides
choices.why: Grignard reagents are made from organohalides and magnesium metal (Section 10.6).

explanation: The Suzuki–Miyaura reaction is particularly useful for preparing biaryl compounds, which have two linked aromatic rings. Many drugs fit this description: the synthesis of valsartan (Diovan), used to treat high blood pressure, begins with a Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of ortho-chlorobenzonitrile with para-methylbenzeneboronic acid.

prompt: Which sequence converts 1-bromobutane into octane using an organocopper coupling?

choices.text: 1. Li; 2. CuI; 3. CH3CH2CH2CH2Br
1. Mg, ether; 2. H2O
choices.why: The Grignard reagent is protonated by water, giving butane, not octane.

choices.text: 1. Li; 2. CuI; 3. CH3CH2Br
choices.why: Coupling a butyl group with an ethyl group gives hexane. You need a second butyl group, from 1-bromobutane.

choices.text: 1. NBS, light; 2. (CH3)2CuLi
choices.why: At most this could add one carbon. Octane needs two four-carbon groups joined together.

explanation: Lithium converts 1-bromobutane into butyllithium; CuI converts that into lithium dibutylcopper; and coupling with a second molecule of 1-bromobutane joins two four-carbon groups to give octane (Exercise 10.7.1b).

prompt: Which two-step sequence converts cyclohexene into 3-methylcyclohexene?

choices.text: 1. NBS, light; 2. (CH3)2CuLi
1. HBr; 2. (CH3)2CuLi
choices.why: HBr adds across the double bond, so coupling would give methylcyclohexane, with no double bond.

choices.text: 1. Br2; 2. (CH3)2CuLi
choices.why: Br2 adds across the double bond to give a 1,2-dibromide, so the double bond is lost.

choices.text: 1. NBS, light; 2. Mg, ether, then H2O
choices.why: Protonating the Grignard reagent replaces Br with H and gives back cyclohexene, with no methyl group.

explanation: NBS brominates the allylic position to give 3-bromocyclohexene, and lithium dimethylcopper then replaces the bromine with a methyl group, giving 3-methylcyclohexene (Exercise 10.7.1a).
